## Why Negative Binomial Regression? {.dark}

```{r}
#| results: asis
#| echo: false
library(jsonlite)
library(MASS)
weekly <- read.csv("data/mosquito_weekly.csv", check.names = FALSE)
pivot <- read.csv("data/pivot_weekly_eggs.csv", check.names = FALSE)
weekly$date <- as.character(weekly$date)
pivot$date <- as.character(pivot[["Fecha Hasta"]])
model_data <- merge(weekly, pivot[, c("date", "Total Eggs", "Sensor Counts")], by = "date")
model_data <- model_data[complete.cases(model_data[, c("Total Eggs", "Sensor Counts", "temperature")]) & model_data[["Sensor Counts"]] > 0, ]
temp_nb <- glm.nb(`Total Eggs` ~ temperature + offset(log(`Sensor Counts`)), data = model_data)
model_data$predicted_total <- predict(temp_nb, type = "response")
model_data$observed_rate <- model_data[["Total Eggs"]] / model_data[["Sensor Counts"]]
model_data$predicted_rate <- model_data$predicted_total / model_data[["Sensor Counts"]]
traps <- paste(readLines("data/ovitraps.geojson", warn = FALSE), collapse = "")
boundary <- paste(readLines("data/study-area.geojson", warn = FALSE), collapse = "")
cat(sprintf(
  '<script>window.deckWeekly=%s;window.deckModel=%s;window.deckTraps=%s;window.deckBoundary=%s;</script>',
  toJSON(weekly, dataframe = "rows", na = "null", auto_unbox = TRUE),
  toJSON(model_data, dataframe = "rows", na = "null", auto_unbox = TRUE),
  traps, boundary
))
```

<div class="hero-grid">
  <div>
    <p class="kicker">Mosquito eggs · count regression · almost no math</p>
    <h1 class="hero-title">How do we choose a model<em>for discrete, overdispersed counts?</em></h1>
    <p class="hero-sub">A practical path from predictors to a Negative Binomial GLM.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="chart-wrap short"><svg id="hero-spark"></svg></div>
</div>

::: {.notes}
I want a model that uses environmental predictors to reproduce systematic variation in mosquito egg abundance. The response is a non-negative count, and it varies much more than a simple Poisson process would allow. This video explains how those two facts lead to Negative Binomial regression.

[Sources]
- User-provided `mosquito_weekly.csv`.
:::

## The question is: under what conditions do expected egg counts change?

<div class="predictor-sequence">
  <div class="predictor primary"><strong>Temperature</strong><span>Begin with one predictor</span></div>
  <div class="predictor-arrow fragment">→</div>
  <div class="response-node fragment"><span>Response variable</span><strong>Expected mosquito egg count</strong></div>
</div>
<div class="more-predictors">
  <div class="predictor fragment"><strong>+ Vapor pressure</strong><span>A second predictor could be added</span></div>
  <div class="predictor fragment"><strong>+ Rainfall</strong><span>Or even more predictors</span></div>
</div>

<span class="slide-footer">03 · Predictors and response</span>

::: {.notes}
Regression connects a response variable to predictors. Temperature, rainfall, vapor pressure, or other variables may enter a multiple-predictor model. To keep the mechanics visible, I will use temperature alone in the worked example.

[Sources]
- User-provided `mosquito_weekly.csv` predictor fields.
:::

## Inspect the response—and how it relates to the predictor

<div class="two-chart-grid">
  <div><p class="small-label">Distribution of weekly egg rates</p><svg id="egg-hist"></svg><p class="chart-takeaway">Bounded at zero, right-skewed · raw variance/mean = 55.7</p></div>
  <div><p class="small-label">Egg rate versus temperature</p><svg id="temp-scatter"></svg><p class="chart-takeaway">The relationship may be nonlinear—and the spread changes</p></div>
</div>
<button class="return-link" onclick="history.back()">← Return to the model</button>

<span class="slide-footer">04 · Explore the response structure</span>

::: {.notes}
The histogram shows a non-negative, right-skewed response, and its raw variance-to-mean ratio is about 55.7. The scatter plot shows that variability is not constant across temperature. These are descriptive warnings rather than proof by themselves. After fitting the temperature-only Poisson model with a valid-trap offset, the Pearson dispersion ratio was approximately 869, confirming severe conditional overdispersion.

[Sources]
- User-provided `mosquito_weekly.csv`; plots use `total_mean_eggs` and `temperature`, and the raw ratio is calculated from non-missing egg-rate observations.
- Hilbe, J. M. (2011), Negative Binomial Regression.
:::

## Ordinary linear regression is a poor match for this response

<div class="two-col">
  <div>
    <p class="kicker">A Gaussian linear model</p>
    <div class="formula">Expected eggs = β₀ + β₁ × temperature</div>
    <p class="dek" style="margin-top:30px">Its line can cross below zero, while its usual error model expects symmetric, constant spread.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="center">
    <p class="small-label">A possible extrapolated prediction</p>
    <p class="impossible-number">−18</p>
    <p style="font-size:34px">expected eggs</p>
    <p class="warning fragment">Negative expected abundance is biologically impossible.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<span class="slide-footer">05 · Why not ordinary linear regression?</span>

::: {.notes}
The issue is not that linear regression can never be used with count-like data. The issue is that its default mean and error structure do not respect what we just saw: a non-negative, skewed response whose spread changes. It can also extrapolate to negative expected counts.

[Sources]
- McCullagh, P. & Nelder, J. A. (1989), Generalized Linear Models.
:::

## Start with a linear model—then generalize it {.dark}

<div class="name-animation">
  <span>Linear Model</span>
  <span class="fragment glm-expanded" data-fragment-index="0"><b>Generalized</b><i>Linear Model</i></span>
  <span class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1">GLM</span>
</div>
<p class="big-claim center fragment" style="margin:70px auto 0;color:var(--lime);font-size:52px">Keep the regression idea. Change the parts that describe the response.</p>

<span class="slide-footer">06 · From LM to GLM</span>

::: {.notes}
A generalized linear model keeps the familiar idea of predictors explaining an expected response. It generalizes the linear model by allowing other outcome distributions and a link between the linear predictor and the mean.

[Sources]
- McCullagh, P. & Nelder, J. A. (1989), Generalized Linear Models.
:::

## Think of a GLM as a toolbox with four connected choices {.dark}

<div class="four-col toolbox" style="margin-top:95px">
  <div class="flat-box fragment"><p class="small-label">01</p><h3>Distribution</h3><p>How does the response vary around its mean?</p></div>
  <div class="flat-box fragment"><p class="small-label">02</p><h3>Linear predictor</h3><p>Which variables explain the response?</p></div>
  <div class="flat-box fragment"><p class="small-label">03</p><h3>Link function</h3><p>How is the mean connected to predictors?</p></div>
  <div class="flat-box fragment"><p class="small-label">04</p><h3>Offset</h3><p>How do we account for unequal exposure?</p></div>
</div>
<div class="toolbox-icon fragment" aria-label="toolbox">🧰</div>

<span class="slide-footer">07 · The GLM toolbox</span>

::: {.notes}
For this application I need four choices. The distribution describes count variability. The linear predictor contains temperature. The link connects that predictor to the expected count. The offset accounts for the number of functioning traps. Strictly speaking, the offset is part of the linear predictor, but it is useful to show it separately because its coefficient is fixed.

[Sources]
- McCullagh, P. & Nelder, J. A. (1989), Generalized Linear Models.
:::

## For count data, Poisson regression is the classic starting point

<div class="two-col" style="margin-top:70px">
  <div><p class="big-claim">The response can be</p><p class="count-sequence">0, 1, 2, 3, …</p><p class="dek">Non-negative integers with no fixed upper limit.</p></div>
  <div><div class="formula formula-large">Yᵢ | Xᵢ ∼ Poisson(μᵢ)</div><div class="symbol-key"><p><strong>Yᵢ</strong> = observed egg count in week i</p><p><strong>Xᵢ</strong> = predictor values in week i</p><p><strong>μᵢ</strong> = expected egg count given Xᵢ</p></div></div>
</div>

<span class="slide-footer">08 · Poisson as the benchmark</span>

::: {.notes}
Poisson regression is the classic benchmark for an unbounded non-negative count. Here Y i is the observed egg count for week i. Mu i is the expected count for week i, conditional on the predictors X i.

[Sources]
- McCullagh, P. & Nelder, J. A. (1989), Generalized Linear Models.
:::

## Poisson makes a strong conditional mean–variance assumption

<div class="formula formula-large center" style="max-width:1250px;margin:35px auto 0">Variance(Yᵢ | Xᵢ) = Mean(Yᵢ | Xᵢ) = μᵢ</div>
<div class="mean-spread">
  <div class="spread-panel"><h3>Poisson-like spread</h3><div class="dotline"><i></i><i></i><i></i><i></i><i></i><i></i><i></i></div><p class="explain center">Counts stay relatively close to the same conditional mean.</p></div>
  <div class="spread-panel fragment"><h3>Extra-Poisson spread</h3><div class="dotline messy"><i></i><i></i><i></i><i></i><i></i><i></i><i></i></div><p class="explain center">The same conditional mean can coexist with much wider variation.</p></div>
</div>
<a class="jump-link" href="#/inspect-the-responseand-how-it-relates-to-the-predictor">↗ Compare this assumption with our response</a>

<span class="slide-footer">09 · The Poisson constraint</span>

::: {.notes}
This equality is conditional: after the predictors are accounted for, Poisson ties the residual variance to the expected count. In the fitted temperature-only Poisson model with the valid-trap offset, the Pearson dispersion ratio was approximately 869. The remaining variation was therefore far beyond what the Poisson model could accommodate, strongly supporting Negative Binomial regression.

[Sources]
- Hilbe, J. M. (2011), Negative Binomial Regression.
:::

## Negative Binomial gives overdispersed counts more room

<div class="two-col" style="margin-top:70px">
  <div><p class="kicker">Poisson</p><div class="formula">Variance = μᵢ</div><p class="dek" style="margin-top:28px">The mean fixes the conditional variance.</p></div>
  <div class="fragment"><p class="kicker">Negative Binomial</p><div class="formula">Variance = μᵢ + αμᵢ²</div><p class="dek" style="margin-top:28px"><strong class="warning">α</strong> is an extra dispersion parameter.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="big-claim fragment center cute-line" style="margin:85px auto 0;font-size:50px">“Negative” is just its surname—it only hangs out with positive counts, plus the occasional zero. 😊</p>

<span class="slide-footer">10 · Choose Negative Binomial</span>

::: {.notes}
Negative Binomial regression relaxes the Poisson variance restriction by adding alpha. If alpha approaches zero, the variance approaches the Poisson variance. The name does not imply negative egg counts.

[Sources]
- Hilbe, J. M. (2011), Negative Binomial Regression.
:::

## The log link connects temperature to a positive expected count

<div class="two-col" style="margin-top:55px">
  <div><p class="small-label">Linear on the log-mean scale</p><div class="formula formula-large">log(μᵢ) = β₀ + β₁ temperatureᵢ</div><p class="explain" style="margin-top:26px"><strong>μᵢ</strong> = expected egg count in week i.</p></div>
  <div class="fragment"><p class="small-label">Transform back to the count scale</p><div class="formula formula-large">μᵢ = exp(β₀ + β₁ temperatureᵢ) &gt; 0</div><p class="explain" style="margin-top:26px">The expected count cannot fall below zero.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="big-claim fragment center" style="margin:85px auto 0;font-size:49px">We link the <span class="warning">expected count</span>—we do not log-transform the observed egg counts.</p>
<a class="jump-link" href="#/inspect-the-responseand-how-it-relates-to-the-predictor">↗ Revisit the nonlinear temperature pattern</a>

<span class="slide-footer">11 · Choose the log link</span>

::: {.notes}
Mu i is the expected egg count for week i. The log link makes that mean linear in temperature on the log scale. Exponentiating returns to the original scale and guarantees a positive expected count. Zero observed counts remain perfectly valid.

[Sources]
- McCullagh, P. & Nelder, J. A. (1989), Generalized Linear Models.
:::

## With a log link, temperature effects are multiplicative

<div class="flow" style="margin-top:95px">
  <div class="flow-node fragment"><strong>Estimated temperature coefficient</strong><span>β₁ = 0.2475</span></div><div class="flow-arrow fragment">→</div><div class="flow-node fragment"><strong>Exponentiate</strong><span>e⁰·²⁴⁷⁵</span></div><div class="flow-arrow fragment">→</div><div class="flow-node fragment" style="border-color:var(--orange)"><strong>Rate ratio = 1.281</strong><span>About 28.1% higher expected count per 1°C increase</span></div>
</div>
<p class="dek fragment center" style="margin:75px auto 0">With temperature alone, this is simply the temperature relationship. If we add more predictors, interpret it while holding those other predictors constant.</p>

<span class="slide-footer">12 · Interpret the coefficient</span>

::: {.notes}
The fitted temperature-only Negative Binomial model estimated a temperature coefficient of 0.2475. Exponentiating gives a rate ratio of 1.281, corresponding to about a 28.1 percent higher expected egg rate per one-degree-Celsius increase. If NDVI or vapor pressure is later added, the temperature effect becomes an adjusted—or conditional—comparison between weeks with the same values of those other predictors. Because strong residual temporal autocorrelation remains, this estimate is presented as the result of the simple first model rather than a final ecological conclusion.

[Sources]
- McCullagh, P. & Nelder, J. A. (1989), Generalized Linear Models.
:::

## Raw totals are not comparable when sampling effort changes

<div class="offset-grid" style="margin-top:55px">
  <div class="week-panel"><p class="small-label">Week A</p><h3>10 valid traps</h3><p class="raw">500 eggs</p><p class="trap-count">500 ÷ 10</p><p class="rate">50 eggs / trap</p></div>
  <div class="versus">versus</div>
  <div class="week-panel fragment"><p class="small-label">Week B</p><h3>20 valid traps</h3><p class="raw">800 eggs</p><p class="trap-count">800 ÷ 20</p><p class="rate">40 eggs / trap</p></div>
</div>
<p class="big-claim fragment center" style="font-size:48px;margin:50px auto 0">More eggs can simply mean more traps were working.</p>
<a class="jump-link sampling-jump" href="#/thirty-four-traps-turn-a-city-into-a-monitoring-network">↗ Revisit the weekly monitoring network</a>

<span class="slide-footer">13 · Unequal exposure</span>

::: {.notes}
Raw totals mix mosquito abundance with sampling opportunity. Week B collected more eggs, but Week A had a higher rate per functioning trap. We therefore need to account for exposure.

[Sources]
- Illustrative sampling-effort example created for this presentation.
:::

## The offset represents opportunity—not a biological effect

<div class="two-col" style="margin-top:50px">
  <div><div class="formula formula-large">log(μᵢ) = β₀ + β₁ temperatureᵢ + 1 × log(valid trapsᵢ)</div><p class="dek" style="margin-top:28px">The coefficient of the offset is fixed at one.</p></div>
  <div class="fragment"><div class="formula formula-large">μᵢ = valid trapsᵢ × exp(β₀ + β₁ temperatureᵢ)</div><p class="dek" style="margin-top:28px">At the same temperature, twice the functioning traps means twice the expected opportunity to collect eggs.</p></div>
</div>

<span class="slide-footer">14 · Choose the offset</span>

::: {.notes}
The logarithm of valid traps enters as an offset. Its coefficient is fixed rather than estimated as a biological predictor effect. This converts the model of totals into a comparison of expected egg abundance per unit of sampling effort.

[Sources]
- Hilbe, J. M. (2011), Negative Binomial Regression.
:::

## The model is four decisions in a deliberate order {.dark}

<div class="model-order">
  <div class="recap-item fragment"><span>1 · Predictor</span><strong>Temperatureᵢ</strong></div>
  <div class="recap-arrow fragment">→</div>
  <div class="recap-item fragment"><span>2 · Distribution</span><strong>Negative Binomial</strong></div>
  <div class="recap-arrow fragment">→</div>
  <div class="recap-item fragment"><span>3 · Link</span><strong>Log</strong></div>
  <div class="recap-arrow fragment">→</div>
  <div class="recap-item fragment"><span>4 · Exposure</span><strong>Offset: valid traps</strong></div>
</div>
<div class="model-formulas fragment">
  <div class="formula formula-large center">Yᵢ ∼ Negative Binomial(μᵢ, α)</div>
  <div class="formula formula-large center">log(μᵢ) = β₀ + β₁ temperatureᵢ + log(valid trapsᵢ)</div>
</div>

<span class="slide-footer">15 · The complete example</span>

::: {.notes}
The example now contains only what we introduced. Temperature is the predictor. Negative Binomial is the distribution. Log is the link. Valid traps form the offset. Additional predictors such as vapor pressure can be added later, but there is no unintroduced time spline in this version.

[Sources]
- User-described modeling objective and sampling design.
- Hilbe, J. M. (2011), Negative Binomial Regression.
:::

## Look at the same temperature-only model in two ways

<div class="two-chart-grid final-charts">
  <div><p class="small-label">Expected rate across temperature</p><svg id="temperature-fit"></svg><p class="chart-takeaway">What the model learns about temperature</p></div>
  <div><p class="small-label">Observed and predicted through time</p><svg id="temporal-fit"></svg><p class="chart-takeaway">Where a one-predictor model still misses structure</p></div>
</div>

<span class="slide-footer">16 · Check the model from two angles</span>

::: {.notes}
Both plots come from the same temperature-only Negative Binomial model with the logarithm of functioning traps as an offset. The left plot isolates the learned relationship with temperature. The right plot puts observations and predictions back in temporal order, making periods of under- and over-prediction easier to see.

[Sources]
- User-provided `mosquito_weekly.csv` and `pivot_weekly_eggs.csv`; temperature-only Negative Binomial model fitted for this presentation using a log offset for `Sensor Counts`.
:::

## One predictor is a beginning—not the final answer {.dark}

<div class="continue-stage">
  <div class="continue-main"><span>Start here</span><strong>Temperature</strong></div>
  <div class="continue-plus fragment">+</div>
  <div class="continue-option fragment"><span>Test next</span><strong>Vapor pressure</strong></div>
  <div class="continue-plus fragment">+</div>
  <div class="continue-option fragment"><span>And perhaps</span><strong>NDVI</strong></div>
</div>
<p class="big-claim center fragment" style="margin:72px auto 0;color:var(--lime);font-size:50px">To be continued: more predictors—and the residual temporal autocorrelation that still remains.</p>

<span class="slide-footer">17 · To be continued</span>

::: {.notes}
Temperature gives us a transparent first model, not necessarily the best final model. The next step is to add vapor pressure, NDVI, or other biologically motivated predictors and assess whether they improve interpretation and out-of-sample prediction. The Negative Binomial model reduced the dispersion problem substantially, but Pearson residuals still had strong temporal dependence: lag-one correlation was approximately 0.64 and the Ljung–Box test was highly significant. The next episode will discuss both predictor expansion and the remaining residual autocorrelation.

[Sources]
- User-provided `mosquito_weekly.csv` predictor fields.
:::
